overview: The atlas calls this 1200 to 1279 feature “Kamarupa,” yet its polygon misses Guwahati, Kamakhya, Hajo, Tezpur, and the old kingdom's Brahmaputra core. Instead it covers tested Kohima, Ukhrul, Myitkyina, and Lijiang, reaching from hill country into northern Myanmar and Yunnan. That is an identity collision, not a medieval border. Historical Kamarupa's great dynastic sequence had already broken apart. In the thirteenth century, western rulers faced armies from Bengal and reorganized toward Kamata; landholding chiefs and other regional powers persisted; Tai-speaking settlers under Siu-ka-pha founded a small eastern realm; Kachari, Chutiya, Bhuyan, and many hill communities followed distinct paths. A North Guwahati rock inscription remembers an invading force's destruction in 1205-06, while Ambari archaeology reveals habitation and craft activity without naming a single ruler. Ordinary people grew food, worked, worshipped, traveled, raised children, and coped with a river landscape, but sources rarely record their voices. This card marks what is known and says plainly when family life, schooling, medicine, sanitation, or toilets disappear from view. At 1279 the map swaps distant eastern places into Pagan and Yuan colors. Assam did not vanish because the software changed crayons.

periods.title: 1200 to 1205: a kingdom-name after dynastic fracture
periods.summary: The atlas begins a Kamarupa feature, but the historical evidence describes no restored valley-wide monarchy. Later compilations reconstruct Prithu or Bartu around this time with real uncertainty. The exact polygon is farther east than the old Guwahati-centered core, so its opening date cannot establish either ruler or frontier.

periods.title: 1205 to 1206: the Kanai Borosibowa inscription
periods.summary: A Sanskrit rock inscription at North Guwahati dates an invading force's destruction to Saka 1127, conventionally 1205-06 CE. It names Kamarupa and the Turushkas but no defending king. The monument therefore secures an event and place better than later attempts to attach a particular hero.

periods.title: 1206 to 1226: recovery without a clear royal list
periods.summary: Narrative sources say Bakhtiyar Khalji's surviving force retreated after its failed Tibet expedition. For the next two decades, rulers and exact domains remain hard to reconstruct. Sparse inscriptions and later chronicles do not justify filling every blank with one continuous Kamarupa dynasty or extending it to Yunnan.

periods.title: 1226 to 1228: renewed western campaigns
periods.summary: A historical synthesis places Ghiyasuddin Iwaz's unsuccessful campaign around 1226, followed by Nasiruddin's intervention and Prithu's fall in the traditional sequence. Names, dates, and identifications vary across later accounts, so this short period should be read as contested frontier warfare rather than a tidy royal handoff.

periods.title: 1228 to 1251: several centers take shape
periods.summary: The conventional Ahom chronology begins Siu-ka-pha's westward migration in 1228, but his initial foothold was a small eastern polity, not all Assam. In the west, Sandhya's chronology is approximate. Between them stood communities and chiefs whom no single Kamarupa label adequately contains.

periods.title: 1251 to 1257: Charaideo and an eastern foothold
periods.summary: The Charaideo dossier places Siu-ka-pha's capital there in 1251 and describes a compact realm bounded by rivers and the Patkai hills. Wet-rice cultivation and royal shrines mattered at this eastern center. None of that makes Charaideo part of the atlas polygon, which actually excludes it.

periods.title: 1257 to 1268: Yuzbak defeated, Kamata emerging
periods.summary: Sources place Malik Yuzbak's invasion and death around 1257, then associate Sandhya with a westward move toward Kamatapur. Acharyya warns that early Kamata reign lengths are reconstructed roughly from later texts and fixed invasions. A reorganization is credible; its exact date and borders remain uncertain.

periods.title: 1268 to 1279: succession, burial, and no common ending
periods.summary: Siu-ka-pha died in 1268 and Charaideo became a dynastic burial place. Western Kamata and other Brahmaputra Valley polities continued independently. By 1279 there was still no single Kamarupa state spanning the atlas shape, and the map endpoint records no shared conquest, collapse, or migration.

sections.title: Read the map before the kingdom

items.text: The live index contains exactly one “kamarupa-1200” record, marked circa and running from 1200 to 1279. Coverage finds one feature in one border file. Those are precise facts about the atlas database, while the name and dates remain an approximate editorial choice rather than a contemporary constitution.

The sole decoded feature is one polygon with one ring and nine positions, bounded roughly by 93.71 to 101.22 degrees east and 24.95 to 28.69 north. Its simplicity signals broad cartographic generalization. No medieval surveyor supplied this clean outline, and no source identifies it as a treaty frontier.

Guwahati, Kamakhya, Hajo, Goalpara, Tezpur, and Nagaon all test outside the Kamarupa polygon. So do Charaideo and Sivasagar in the eastern Brahmaputra Valley. A shape that excludes both the old western core and the early Ahom center cannot safely represent thirteenth-century Assam.

Kohima, Ukhrul, Myitkyina, and Lijiang test inside the target. Imphal, Putao, Tengchong, Dali, and Bhamo test outside. This peculiar selection crosses modern India, Myanmar, and China while slicing through neighboring uplands, evidence of a misplaced imported geometry rather than a coherent historical region.

The polygon shares imported arcs with Tibet, Song dynasty, Nan Chao, Bagan, and Bhutan labels. Shared arcs explain how the picture was tiled; they do not prove diplomacy or contact. The audit treats every border as a display artifact until independent history supports a relationship, which here it often does not.

Acharyya's chapter calls the early Kamrup or Kamata royal dates rough estimates because later local chronicles do not arrange them chronologically. That warning matters: a neat list from Prithu to Sandhya can look firmer than its evidence. The card therefore marks rulers and transitions circa rather than manufacturing birthdays for reigns.

Regional historical syntheses describe early thirteenth-century Kamrup as politically fragmented, with new states and armed landholding chiefs coexisting. That model fits the evidence better than the atlas blob. Fragmented does not mean empty or chaotic; it means authority was distributed among several kinds of rulers and communities.

Western Kamarupa was reorganized toward Kamata, but even the educational synthesis notes disagreement over whether Prithu or Sandhya should count as founder. The safe conclusion is a westward political re-centering during the century, not a single exact coronation that instantly renamed every village from Guwahati to Kamatapur.

In the east, Siu-ka-pha's followers established a compact Tai-Ahom polity, while older Kachari, Chutiya, Bhuyan, and hill societies retained their own leaders and territories. “Assam” later became a wider political name, but applying that later unity backward would erase the very diversity that shaped the thirteenth century.

The imported summary describes ancient Kamarupa, whose major dynasties belong mostly before this card's interval. It cannot serve as evidence for a state after 1200. Repeating it would turn chronological overlap into continuity, much like assuming a family still owns a house because an old mailbox kept the surname.

The Kanai Borosibowa record says that Turushkas came to Kamarupa and met destruction in Saka 1127. It does not mention Prithu, Bakhtiyar, army size, battlefield tactics, or a rescuing dynasty. Those details come from other narratives and later identifications, so the inscription must not be made to say more than it carved.

The rock-art field team places Kanai Barasi on a low hill beside the Brahmaputra and records inscriptions from 1206 and 1665 on the same site. Multiple periods literally share the rocks. That is a useful reminder that a monument can accumulate memories without every carving describing one continuous kingdom.

Later histories connect the 1205-06 disaster with Bakhtiyar Khalji's Tibet expedition and the 1226 campaign with Ghiyasuddin Iwaz. These accounts help reconstruct sequence, but the earliest local inscription records only an outcome. Responsible storytelling distinguishes the securely carved sentence from the larger narrative assembled around it.

The 1257 campaign of Malik Yuzbak ended in defeat and his death, with rain and flooding prominent in the narrative tradition. The episode shows how armies moving through a river-and-hill landscape faced environmental risks as well as defenders. It does not prove that floods were deliberately commanded by a single king.

An official district history repeats the conventional Prithu-Sandhya succession and invasion sequence. Because district handbooks summarize rather than re-edit primary texts, this card uses it as evidence for a durable historical tradition, not as the final judge of disputed names, precise reign dates, or territorial reach.

Ambari in modern Guwahati has a later occupation phase spanning roughly the thirteenth through seventeenth centuries. Excavators found floors and hearths, while broader work found brick pathways and structural remains. These are real traces of settled activity near the old core, although their broad dating rarely isolates 1200 to 1279.

Ambari pottery includes wheel-turned kaolin, red, buff, and some grey wares, with a smaller handmade component. Pots imply storage, cooking, serving, production, and exchange, but a sherd cannot identify its user's language, religion, or ruler. Archaeology answers some daily questions while refusing several tempting ones.

Ambari excavation records include structural remains and material that indicate occupied space. Their dating is not narrow enough to assign them confidently to a family in this exact interval. Even so, archaeology can reveal domestic settings where chronicles mostly offer kings and battles.

Government heritage summaries divide Ambari into seventh-to-twelfth and thirteenth-to-seventeenth-century phases. That boundary places the site beside this card's interval, but it is not a stopwatch: deposits can mix and structures can be reused. “Medieval layer” is useful context, not permission to date every bead to 1234.

A Nataraja sculpture found at Ambari is catalogued by the Assam State Museum to about the thirteenth or fourteenth century. Its findspot and date demonstrate continuing skilled stonework near Guwahati. They do not identify the sculptor, patron, workshop wages, or exact year, all of which remain wonderfully frustrating blanks.

Charaideo's official history associates Siu-ka-pha's settlement with wet-rice cultivation and a flood-sheltered site. That evidence belongs to a small eastern polity, not the atlas polygon and not every household. Rice was important, but sources do not provide a dependable 1200-to-1279 menu for all western, central, eastern, and hill communities.

Older regional histories describe early Ahom settlement as agricultural and connected with neighboring villages, while later economic historians distinguish settled fields from shifting cultivation. The mixed picture cautions against imagining one uniform farm system across a valley whose soils, floods, slopes, and political obligations varied.

Kaolin pottery had circulated around the Brahmaputra Valley before 1200, and the Ambari sequence used it through its earlier phase. Because the cited archaeological report's range ends in the twelfth century, this card treats it as inherited craft background rather than automatically carrying every vessel into the thirteenth.

Assam's industries history records long regional traditions of pottery and riverbed gold washing, but it does not securely date particular workshops to 1200-1279. Such traditions can suggest questions for archaeology; they cannot turn a later craft description into a day in Prithu's marketplace. Chronology gets the last word.

Ambari yielded ceramics associated with long-distance connections, including celadon and green-glazed wares. Their broad archaeological phases do not isolate a shipment in 1200-1279. Those finds show the site's wide horizons across time, not a securely dated thirteenth-century import ledger or a merchant's named itinerary.

The Charaideo dossier says Siu-ka-pha crossed the Patkai with family members as well as soldiers and followers. That is rare direct acknowledgment that migration was more than an army's march. It still does not tell us household size, marriage patterns, children's ages, inheritance, or women's decisions among the communities encountered.

Ahom was one Southwestern Tai language within a multilingual population that already included several Tibeto-Burman-speaking groups. Daily communication therefore likely required translation, accommodation, or multilingual practice, though the sources do not map who spoke what at each hearth. A political label never makes every grandmother use the same vocabulary.

The early polity included nobles, priests, followers, and neighboring villages with unequal relationships. Later institutional patterns cannot simply be pasted onto its first decades. The surviving summaries describe offices and royal action more readily than affection, quarrels, adoption, disability, or care work within ordinary families. Those absences are historical evidence too.

Royal burial at Charaideo eventually included rulers and other elites, with rites expressing status and ancestry. The surviving tradition is evidence for court belief, not a census of common funerals. Poorer families, mobile groups, and western communities may have commemorated the dead in ways the monuments have not recovered.

No source used here supplies a representative thirteenth-century marriage contract, household register, diary, or oral testimony from a woman or child. The card therefore avoids claims that all marriages were arranged, all households were patriarchal, or women held one fixed status across Kachari, Bhuyan, Tai, and other societies.

Children scarcely appear in the surviving political and archaeological record: there are no secure lessons, games, age grades, apprenticeships, or discipline manuals for 1200-1279. Skills were certainly transmitted somehow; saying exactly how would require evidence we do not possess. The school bell, if any, is archaeologically silent.

Later Ahom chronicles, or buranjis, preserve early narratives, yet their chronology must be tested rather than accepted mechanically. Astronomical analysis of chronicle references demonstrates one method of checking dates. For this card, later narrative memory is valuable evidence with a long transmission history, not a live report filed in 1228.

Ahom later served court and ritual functions and was the mother tongue of part of a multilingual population. The Cambridge account does not prove how much was written in Siu-ka-pha's lifetime or who could read it. Spoken language, ritual literacy, and administrative writing must be kept separate rather than bundled as “education.”

The epigraphic record between the mid-twelfth century and later medieval chronicles is notably thin. That gap explains why one short rock inscription carries unusual weight. It also warns against treating silence as illiteracy: writing may have occurred on materials that decayed, remained undiscovered, or were never preserved by courts.

No securely dated school building, pupil list, curriculum, exercise tablet, or child's writing sample from 1200-1279 appears in the surveyed sources. Elite Sanskrit inscription and later Tai court traditions show specialized literacy, while education for most children remains unknown. Family teaching and apprenticeship are plausible, but not documented here.

Written-language sample, normalized Devanagari Sanskrit: “शाके तुरगयुग्मेशे मधुमासत्रयोदशे । कामरूपं समागत्य तुरुष्काः क्षयमाययुः ॥” Transliteration: “śāke turaga-yugmeśe madhumāsa-trayodaśe | kāmarūpaṃ samāgatya turuṣkāḥ kṣayam āyayuḥ ||” Translation: “In Saka 1127, on the thirteenth day of the spring month, the Turks came to Kamarupa and met destruction.”

Date, place, and genre: this is a victory record cut on rock at Kanai Borosibowa in North Guwahati, dated Saka 1127, conventionally 1205-06 CE. Published conversions differ by a year or exact modern day, so the card retains the era date and a cautious CE range.

Script note: published epigraphic study treats the carving within eastern inscription traditions. The displayed line is a modern Unicode Devanagari normalization of its Sanskrit, not a tracing of weathered regional letterforms. Transliteration preserves the edited words but cannot reproduce the stonecutter's hand.

The formula uses a chronogram for the Saka year rather than ordinary written numerals. That clever dating device makes the line both text and puzzle, although modern editors disagree slightly on segmentation and spelling. The safest classroom sample shows one normalized reading and tells children that epigraphers still compare letters.

The inscription's “Kamarupa” is historical evidence for a regional name at North Guwahati. Ironically, North Guwahati lies outside the atlas target polygon. The very writing sample that anchors the card therefore disproves a literal reading of the shape: the name survives where the colored feature does not reach.

No surveyed source securely identifies a physician, medical school, hospital, pharmacy, surgical kit, or named treatment in this exact region and interval. Later evidence cannot be projected backward. People certainly treated illness and injury; the surviving artifact, feature, and text record does not show how.

Ambari excavations found hearths and built floors, useful clues to indoor work and food preparation. They do not reveal whether smoke was managed well, where the sick rested, or who cleaned. A hearth can warm dinner and sting eyes at once; archaeology rarely supplies the household complaint that followed.

The broader Ambari complex includes a brick tank, floors, and other structural remains, but published descriptions do not securely date a sanitation system to 1200-1279. Water management existed at the site across time. It would be unsafe to convert broad remains into a thirteenth-century municipal sewer system.

No excavated toilet or latrine is securely dated here to the exact interval, and no text explains waste disposal, bathing frequency, menstrual care, childbirth hygiene, or drinking-water rules. The honest toilet card is therefore short on fixtures and long on uncertainty. Absence of evidence is not evidence of sparkling bathrooms.

Riverbanks, tanks, wells, rain, and seasonal floods would have shaped water access, but local practices varied and are not documented closely enough for a single routine. Archaeological features show water storage without household instructions. They do not tell us whether ordinary drinking water was filtered, boiled, or shared with animals.

sections.title: What changed, what endured, what we cannot claim

items.text: The most defensible achievement of the century was not one empire's expansion. It was the creation and adaptation of several political centers: Kamata in the west, a new Tai-Ahom foothold in the east, resilient local lordships between them, and communities whose material and religious life continued through invasions and environmental shocks.

Later buranjis became unusually important historical sources, but their early chapters mix transmitted history with origin traditions. A Royal Asiatic Society study traced mythical royal descent alongside chronicle material. Reading these texts critically respects them more than stripping away their genre and turning every ancestral story into GPS data.

Archaeology adds discoveries that royal narratives miss: hearths, floors, pottery, beads, sculptures, tanks, pathways, and workshop debris. Yet objects also have limits. They rarely identify a child's joke, a healer's recipe, or the person assigned latrine duty, which may be why archaeology has fewer volunteers for that last question.

At 1279 the target vanishes. Kohima, Ukhrul, Myitkyina, Imphal, Tengchong, and Bhamo fall under the atlas's Pagan label, while Dali and Lijiang fall under Yuan. Historical Kamarupa's Guwahati core has no target ownership on either side of that seam. This is database relabeling, not synchronized conquest.

The 1300 snapshot repeats the 1279 assignments, confirming a stable editorial regime after the seam. It still says nothing about a common fall in Assam. Kamata, the early Ahom polity, and other regional societies continued on their own timelines, so the card ends with continuity and names no single successor.

ending.text: At 1279 the exact “kamarupa-1200” feature disappears. The atlas reassigns its eastern members to Pagan and Yuan labels, while Guwahati, North Guwahati, Kamakhya, Hajo, Tezpur, Charaideo, and other historical Assam probes were never inside it. No source records a matching conquest, royal death, mass migration, or common political ending. Western Kamata, the small Tai-Ahom realm around Charaideo, Kachari and Chutiya formations, Bhuyan chiefs, and hill communities continued through different chronologies. The override therefore leaves fell null, names no predecessor or successor, and treats 1279 as an editorial seam. People kept farming, making pots, raising children, worshipping, trading, healing as they could, and finding somewhere practical to go to the toilet after the map changed color.
